app.title: Drugs, microbiome and metabolism
app.subtitle: What 2,173 European patients reveal about the hidden footprint of treatments

sidebar.fdr_help: Maximum false discovery rate. 0.05 = at most 5% false positives expected.
sidebar.robust_only_help: Hides associations explained by another factor (country, another drug, BMI...).
sidebar.group_help: "All analyses" includes subgroup analyses; "Pooled analyses" keeps only those run on all patients.
sidebar.help_title: ℹ️ What are these settings for?
sidebar.help:
- **The story**: the steps of the story, to read in order (or not!).
- **FDR threshold**: the **smaller** it is, the more we keep only **very reliable** results (fewer results, but more trustworthy). 0.05 is the standard value.
- **Robust associations only**: when on, links explained by something else (another drug, country, BMI...) are hidden. When off, you see **everything**, including misleading links.
- **Feature type**: choose what to look at (blood and urine molecules, bacterial species, bacterial functions). Click × to remove one.
- **Patient group**: restrict to analyses run within one group (e.g. type 2 diabetes).
- **Reset**: go back to the default settings.

common.no_data: No association matches these filters. Try widening the FDR threshold.

footer.disclaimer: Associations shown are statistical: they do not prove cause and effect and are not medical advice.

intro.title: 1 · Why it matters
intro.question: When we treat a metabolic disease, what do we do to the microbiome and to metabolism?
intro.hook: In cardiometabolic patients, drugs leave a stronger footprint than the disease itself.
intro.context: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, coronary disease: these patients often take **several drugs at once**. Yet these treatments also change **gut bacteria** and **molecules in blood and urine**. The European **MetaCardis** cohort (Forslund *et al.*, *Nature* 2021) measured all three in 2,173 people. This dashboard explores the associations it published.
intro.audience:
- **Students and researchers** in biology, pharmacology, nutrition
- **Clinicians** curious about the off-target effects of treatments
- Anyone who wants to see why **correlation ≠ causation**
intro.questions:
1. Do drugs weigh more than the disease?
2. Which drugs affect which bacteria and metabolites?
3. How many of the observed links are misleading, and why?
intro.map_sub: Number of patients per recruitment country
intro.drugs_sub: Mean number of different drugs per patient, by group
intro.insight_drugs: Patients in the "{group}" group take {n} drugs on average, versus {ctrl} in healthy controls: the disease cannot be studied without accounting for treatments.
intro.usage_sub: Share of patients (%) taking each drug class
intro.caveat_denmark: Age and BMI of the 527 Danish patients are not published (Danish data protection): age and BMI averages cover France and Germany only.
intro.glossary:
- **Gut microbiome**: the billions of bacteria living in our gut. They digest part of our food and produce molecules that can help (or not) our body.
- **Metabolome**: all the small molecules measured in blood and urine (sugars, fats, amino acids...). It is a "snapshot" of our metabolism.
- **Association**: two things that vary together (e.g. patients on metformin have more of a given bacterium). It is **not necessarily a cause**.
- **FDR (false discovery rate)**: when running thousands of tests, some come out "by chance". An FDR of 0.05 means we accept at most 5% false alarms.
- **Effect size**: the strength of the link, from −1 (strong decrease) to +1 (strong increase). 0 = no effect.
- **Confounder**: a third element that explains the link. Example: if diabetic patients all take metformin, an effect attributed to diabetes may actually come from metformin.
- **Robust association**: it still holds after accounting for other factors (other drugs, country, age, BMI...).

network.title: 3 · The interaction network
network.question: Which drugs affect the same bacteria or the same metabolites?
network.how_to_read: **How to read:** each blue diamond is a drug, each symbol a feature it changes. A **red** line = the feature increases, **blue** = it decreases. Features in the **centre** are affected by several drugs: they are the network's "crossroads".
network.chart_sub: Diamonds = drugs · red = increase, blue = decrease · size = number of links
network.insight_shared: {n} features are changed by at least two drugs. The most shared one, "{feature}", is linked to {k} treatments ({drugs}): different drugs can converge on the same biological targets.
network.insight_none: With these settings, no drug shares a feature with another: increase the number of associations per drug.
network.betweenness_help: Betweenness: share of the network's shortest paths that go through this node. High = the drug connects distant parts of the network.
network.caveat: The network only shows each drug's strongest associations (to stay readable): a missing link does not mean a missing effect.

data_quality.title: 6 · Data quality
data_quality.question: Can we trust these numbers? What was checked, fixed, and what is missing.
data_quality.funnel_title: From raw file to clean data
data_quality.funnel_sub: Number of rows after each cleaning step
data_quality.insight_funnel: {removed} rows removed ({pct} of the file): mostly {dup} exact duplicates and {inf} infinite effect sizes.
data_quality.check_md5: Downloaded files identical to Zenodo's (md5 checksum)
data_quality.check_ranges: FDR between 0 and 1, finite effect size (missing FDR: {fdr_missing} · out of range: {fdr_out_of_range} · missing effect: {effect_missing} · infinite effect: {effect_infinite})
data_quality.check_join: Demographics × drugs join checked as one-to-one
data_quality.check_privacy: Privacy: only aggregates are published, no group smaller than 10 patients
data_quality.missing_results_note: These columns only apply to part of the tests: they were dropped.
data_quality.mnar: Missing values are **not random**: age and BMI are missing for 100% of Danish patients (removed to comply with Danish law). Age and BMI averages therefore only represent France and Germany.
data_quality.robust_note: The authors tested whether each association is explained by another factor (another drug, country, BMI...). By default, the app only shows robust associations.
data_quality.assumptions:
- **Key duplicates** (same test, factor, group and feature): the most significant result is kept.
- **"OK" status** classified as robust (consistent with the authors' *metadeconfoundR* tool).
- **Status given as a list of variables** = association confounded by these variables.
- **Polypharmacy**: at least 5 different drugs (usual definition).
- **Network**: only "drug intake" tests are used, to avoid duplicates with doses and combinations.
- **Effect size**: signed value between −1 and 1, as published by the authors.

conclusions.title: 7 · Conclusions & limits
conclusions.question: What to remember, and what these data do not say.
conclusions.k1_text: More than half of the apparent links are explained by **another factor**. Without correction, effects would be wrongly attributed to the disease.
conclusions.k2_text: **Drugs** and the **recruitment country** dominate confounders: they must be accounted for in any microbiome study.
conclusions.k3_text: With the current filters, it is associated with **{n}** microbiome and metabolome features.
conclusions.implications:
- **Research**: any search for microbiome biomarkers must correct for treatments, or it may "discover" a drug effect.
- **Clinical**: a treatment's effects on the microbiome could explain part of its benefits or side effects.
- **Public health**: polypharmacy in cardiometabolic patients calls for studies that analyse drug **combinations**.
conclusions.limits:
- **Correlation ≠ causation**: these are statistical associations from an observational study.
- **Secondary data**: we visualise published results without re-running the statistical tests.
- **Danish patients**: age and BMI not published, which limits demographic comparisons.
- **Unannotated metabolites**: much of the urine and serum metabolome has no chemical name.
- **A single snapshot**: no follow-up over time, so no before/after treatment.
conclusions.next:
- Compare effects **by dose** and **by drug combination** (tests already in the data).
- Cross with a **longitudinal** study (before/after starting treatment).
- Link metabolites to their pathways (KEGG) to interpret the network's crossroads.

my_drug.title: 5 · What about my drug?
my_drug.question: Pick a drug: is its effect stronger than the disease's, and does it really come from the drug?
my_drug.intro: This page answers two questions **in plain language**, for the drug and disease of your choice. Answers follow the sidebar filters.
my_drug.q1: 1. Does {drug} leave a stronger footprint than "{disease}"?
my_drug.v1_stronger: Yes: {drug} changes the microbiome and metabolome more often than the disease itself.
my_drug.v1_similar: Comparable: {drug} and the disease change the microbiome and metabolome to a similar extent.
my_drug.v1_weaker: No: the disease leaves a stronger footprint than {drug}.
my_drug.v1_unknown: Cannot compare: not enough tests for this drug or this disease.
my_drug.m_help: {n} robust associations out of {tested} features tested
my_drug.chart1_sub: Share of tested features that are robustly changed (%)
my_drug.strength: **Strength:** when {drug} changes a feature, the median effect is **{d}** (on a 0 to 1 scale). For "{disease}", it is **{m}**.
my_drug.shared_text: **{n} features** are changed by both {drug} and "{disease}": **{same}** go in the **same direction** (the drug follows or mimics the disease) and **{opp}** in the **opposite direction** (the drug might partly correct what the disease disrupts).
my_drug.q2: 2. Do these effects really come from {drug}?
my_drug.v2_mostly_drug: ✅ Mostly yes: {pct} of {drug}'s effects hold after adjusting for other factors.
my_drug.v2_mostly_other_drugs: 💊 Not always: only {pct} of {drug}'s effects are its own; many are explained by **other drugs** taken at the same time.
my_drug.v2_mostly_environment: 🌍 Not always: only {pct} of {drug}'s effects are its own; many are explained by **the setting** (recruitment country).
my_drug.v2_mostly_patient: 🧍 Not always: only {pct} of {drug}'s effects are its own; many are explained by **patient profile** (age, BMI, sex).
my_drug.v2_mostly_lifestyle: 🥗 Not always: only {pct} of {drug}'s effects are its own; many are explained by **lifestyle** (smoking, diet).
my_drug.v2_mostly_disease: 🩺 Not always: only {pct} of {drug}'s effects are its own; many are explained by **the disease** itself.
my_drug.v2_mixed: 🔀 Mixed: {pct} of {drug}'s effects are its own, the others have various explanations.
my_drug.chart2_title: Where do the effects come from?
my_drug.chart3_sub: % of changed features, by explanation found
my_drug.overlap_note: One effect can have several explanations: percentages can add up to more than 100%.
my_drug.how:
- **Footprint** = share of tested features that are **robustly** changed (FDR below the chosen threshold and not explained by another factor). We compare **rates**, because the drug and the disease were not tested on the same number of features.
- **Stronger / comparable / weaker**: more than a 20% gap between the two rates.
- **Strength**: median absolute effect size of robust associations.
- **Origin of effects**: deconfounding status computed by the study authors (*metadeconfoundR* tool). A "confounded" association is explained by another variable, which we group into 5 families.
my_drug.medical: These results describe **statistical trends in a group of patients**, not a drug's effect in one person. Never change a treatment without medical advice.
